Okay, okay. I'm going to turn it over to Council Member Stevens. Oh, she— sorry, she totally left. Finance Chair, did you have any questions? Okay, all right. I guess that'll be it for you. I mean, obviously we're going to, you know– I think everyone here that's come to this committee wants to see you all keep that one vacant position and certainly want to get you $100,000 more for your OTPS so you can have more lights or printers or whatever you need to get your job done. And just really appreciate the work you're doing. We want to see good people working for the city, and it's not surprising to see that we are not hiring Black workers. I mean, that's kind of the on-par for every other issue going on. So we want to partner with you on that, and let us know how we can be a resource to

you as individual council members to help get the word out in lieu of your tiny budget.
Thank you very much to all of you.
Thank you so much. Thank you.
Thank you.
Okay, we're going to take a quick break and then we will hear from MOERJ. [break]

All right, everyone, we're going to pick this back up. Sorry for the delays. We were also over in our in our time. So it worked out perfectly for a little break. Good afternoon. Again, I'm Council Member Sandy Nurse, Chair of this Committee. I now welcome Afua Atta-Mensah, Commissioner and Chief Equity Officer at the Mayor's Office of Equity and Racial Justice, or MOERJ, for their testimony at this hearing. MOERJ is responsible for advancing racial equity in the city, which includes releasing the racial equity plans– which we know that you are going to release them by the deadline– as well as the true cost of living. MOERJ also consists of various other mayoral offices,

including, NYC Her Future, the New York City Commission on Gender Equity, New York City Unity Project, New York City Young Men's Initiative, New York City Pay Equity Cabinet, and New York City Task Force on Racial Inclusion and Equity. This is the first time MOERJ will testify at our budget hearing. So thank you for coming in. MOERJ’s fiscal year 2027 budget as of the preliminary plan is close to $5.6 million, which includes $4.6 million in personnel services for 38 positions and $1 million in other than personal services. MOERJ's fiscal '26 budget includes two other adjustment reductions for a total of $1 million, which reflects a transfer of funding to other city agencies that partner with MOERJ on their programming. We definitely were— are going to ask about that, and we'd like to hear how you all are partnering with other city agencies, as well as learning about how its budget and headcount are supporting its mandates in this upcoming cycle. So, thank you all for being here. I just want to recognize we've been joined by Council Member Lynn Schulman, and I'm gonna turn it over to Committee Counsel to administer the oath.
Good afternoon. If you could please raise your right hands. Do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before this committee?
Yes.
Yes.
Yes.
Thank you so much. You may begin.

Well, good afternoon, Chair Nurse, members of the Committee on Civil and Human Rights, distinguished members of the council, and of course the public. Thank you for convening this hearing today. As was stated, I am Afua Atta-Mensah. I serve as the city's Chief Equity Officer as well as the Commissioner for the Mayor's Office for Equity and Racial Justice. I am exceedingly joyed to be joined today by members of my team: Delilah Tyson, the Chief Administrative Officer. This is her first time testifying, so everybody talk to her nice today. We also have Latifah Ford, the Executive Director for NYC Her Future, and I believe we will momentarily be joined by Deputy Commissioner Debash Nagash, and we are

excited to speak with you about MOERJ's continued work to advance pay equity in our city. Chairwoman, great minds think alike, so you took so many of my initial talking points in your opening, but I'll just give a little bit of the greatest hits before going into details. As I shared in my earlier testimony a few— when I was before this distinguished panel a few weeks ago, we are the centralized city office that takes the intersectional approach to advance equity across our city. Our mandate is simple. We are rooted in the powerful belief that every New Yorker deserves the opportunity to live, work, and thrive with dignity. In order to realize that vision, we bring together several key initiatives and offices that work across government to tackle inequities experienced by communities in our city. Using various strategies from policy and research to advocacy and programs. As you detailed earlier, that includes the Commission on Gender Equity, which works to ensure the city leads in development and implementation of our best practices in gender equity policies and programs with a focus on economic mobility, health, and safety. The NYC Young Men's Initiative and NYC Her Future sibling offices focus on addressing

inequities amongst young men of color and young women women of color respectively in education, employment, health, and justice. NYC Unity Project works to address inequities amongst LGBTQ+ New Yorkers, particularly youth and people of color. At MOREJ, we take a three-pronged approach to our work with a focus on structural change, which is dismantling the structural inequalities across city government. This includes the implementation of our Racial Justice Charter Mandatees, culture change and engagement, which is breaking silos and shifting culture to increase collaboration and inclusion. This includes bringing stakeholders together in various ways to contribute to shared strategies to advance equity and support community-based coalitions to advance these local initiatives. And also in creating equitable outcomes for New Yorkers, utilizing a whole-of-government approach to address disparities concentrated by race, gender, and other identities. Building the infrastructure for equity in government, as you know, the Charter calls for the city to create the Office of Racial Equity. Following the announcement of this office in the previous fiscal year, months of planning to identify and secure

fiscal resources. This was— excuse me, I should take a step back. This was during fiscal year 2025. And so they were creating preliminary staffing structures, and began establishing personnel and other admin systems necessary to onboard staff and ensure sustainable operations to advance the work. During fiscal year '25, MOERJ also spent significant time implementing its racial equity planning process aimed at moving government towards equity and justice together. In preparation for agency to build their first racial equity plan, MOERJ engaged them in advance of development, which included building racial equity planning teams within each agency, reviewing their priorities relative to the foundational values of the Charter, assessing disparity data, and Commission on Racial Equity, community equity priorities. Also leading full-day workshops in developing and providing planning tools to guide the process. During that time, MOERJ also continued our work with over 40 city agencies and 200+ staff as they began to refine the individual racial equity plan goals, strategies, and indicators with the guidance of the MOERJ team throughout the process. MOERJ has also spent this time now

finalizing plans with agencies and rolling them into a single citywide preliminary racial equity plan, which will be the first for the city. As part of this process, we hired equity planning managers to support racial equity planning, as well as work with agencies on the implementation of the plan. We look forward to publishing this plan within the first 100 days and sharing it with the sector, public, receiving community feedback, and continuing to work together with city agencies and all stakeholders to finalize it for implementation. We've also been diligently working on the true cost of living measure. It has been an important priority for our office. Again, per City Charter, the New York City true cost of living measure established what it costs to meet basic needs in our city and live with dignity without consideration of public, private, or informal assistance. Recognizing the limitations of the federal poverty measure, the true cost of living measure will move beyond basic poverty calculations to capture what it costs to meet basic needs, get through emergencies, and have the financial stability necessary to plan for one's future. This should not be a luxury, and yet it often feels that way to New

Yorkers across this city. This measure will analyze costs across various household sizes, age groups, and essential areas of need to create a comprehensive understanding of what it truly takes to thrive in our city. As one of the first cities to create a measure of this type, the true cost of living measure can help inform us on the local level as well as inform local, state, and national policy priorities to help us further advocate for the needs of working people in this city. To meet the spirit of the Charter, MOERJ has worked in partnership with the Mayor's Office for Economic Opportunity and the Urban Institute to leverage local and national research to best determine costs for New York City across various household sizes, types, age groups, and essential areas of need, incorporate categories critical to economic safety and one's ability to thrive, including debt and savings, and look at costs across various age groups, including individuals with disabilities, as well as other areas of cost such as caregiving. And we look forward to publishing the full report developed by MOERJ and Urban Initiative and others to share the measure in the upcoming weeks. We also remain committed to advancing gender

equity, not only externally for the city's residents, but also internally for the city's workforce. We are proud that the Commission on Gender Equity and the Department of Citywide Administrative Services co-chair the Pay Equity Cabinet, which serves as an oversight body to provide accountability for pay equity goals across the city government workforce. In 2025, the cabinet selected and began working with a vendor to execute a pay equity job title evaluation. The first pay equity analysis report will be published in 2027 and identifies occupational segregation and gender and race pay disparities within civil service titles. This June, the job title evaluation will enter the second year of its four-year project to identify occupational segregation and gender and race pay disparities within the city government workforce. In regards to our programmatic investments, we make these programmatic investments to serve communities that have experienced this disparities and disinvestment to improve outcomes for New Yorkers. And I'll just share a few examples. NYC Her Future, as I previously mentioned, a unit within MOERJ, is created to address the disparities that young women of color in

particular face across New York City in areas of education, employment, justice, and health, as well as to provide them with the tools to be successful by their own definition. Following the launch of NYC Her Future in the previous fiscal year, the unit got right to work to develop and champion programs and partnerships that support the success of young women throughout the city. FY25 programs and partnerships included, but were not limited to, a partnership with CUNY through Health Career Center, which provides vouchers and guidance for participants to pursue health-related certificate programs, helping them to select courses, confirm eligibility, and apply coursework toward academic credit or future degrees. This citywide program served 356 students in FY25 and achieved a 91 percent completion rate. Partnering with the Administration of Children's Services on Future Force, which empowers young women and teens through mentoring, career exploration, vocational training, financial support, and professional development, including coaching workshops and access to mentors. The initiative has provided 57 young people involved in the child welfare system with individualized career coaching, vocational training,

training and full financial support for certifications and materials, as well as a $3,300 completion stipend. Future Force helps address low post-secondary enrollment, limited professional networks, and high unemployment among youth experiencing the foster care system. NYC Her Future is an innovate— is truly an innovation and investment hub within city government and serves as a thought partner and funding catalyst to agencies across New York City, and we look forward to the work it will continue to do to design, pilot, and evaluate initiatives that serve as proof of concept for sustained baseline investment in scalable models that advance gender equity citywide. MOERJ has also continued to invest in the Task Force on Racial Inclusion and Equity, the TRIE Neighborhood Initiative, in collaboration with the Civic Engagement Commission. The TRIE Neighborhood Initiative is a four-year partnership which invests in community-based organizations to strengthen civic engagement and local decision-making. The program was born out of the COVID-19 pandemic through TRIE to address the disparate impacts of COVID-19 on communities of color and support the development of

community networks that could connect residents to one another as well as city government. This initiative is implemented by CEC in partnership with MOERJ and the Young Men's Initiative. In fiscal year '25, 30 community-based organizations were awarded funds to serve as TRIE Neighborhood Ambassadors across 31 TRIE Neighborhoods. And during the program, organizations are tasked with empowering residents to help shape city priorities and resources through civic education and participation in the People's Money. Over the course of each year, each neighborhood convened at least quarterly to discuss the community needs, strategies to engage community members in the People's Money, and opportunities to collaborate and share resources to support one another in the work. TNA conducted 124 meetings throughout the year, and TRIE coalition membership increased to 255 partners from different fields, including nonprofits, local businesses, as well as faith institutions. Civic engagement workshops were also organized to promote civic education and community partnership within TRIE Neighborhoods, and in fiscal year '25, 36 workshops were organized with 730 participants. TNAs were also involved in the

People's Money process, serving as trusted conveners in their communities and in providing an equity lens lens in each phase of the process, including idea generation, facilitating over 160 workshops across communities and generating 1,300 ideas for projects to strengthen their communities, facilitating conversations with coalition members to build consensus and identify the top priorities for their neighborhoods, and engaging over 77,000 residents in the voting process by conducting voting activities in schools, libraries, and older adult centers, mobilizing volunteers to knock on doors and table at events, and present to community boards. Moving to fiscal year 2026, we've continued to build on infrastructure for equity in government. In fiscal year 2026, MOERJ continued operationally to build itself out. We outgrew an existing space and were able to secure larger office space in partnership with DCAS. We also spent significant time preparing to move in, to move in those oper— to move our operation to that new space and engaging with partnership with the Office of Technology Innovation to physically move in and what have you. We've continued programmatic investments, including in

service of LGBT communities as well as with young men of color. This fiscal year, 20 community-based organizations across New York City were selected through a competitive process to receive funding through the city's Transgender, Gender Nonconforming, and Nonbinary Empowerment Fund. This is a $2 million investment designed to strengthen community infrastructure and ensure that TGNCNB New Yorkers across all five boroughs can access essential services. These organizations provide critical support in areas including health and wellness, justice, legal advocacy, youth and family support, violence prevention, and career crisis response, to name a few. Each organization receives up to $92,000 to sustain and expand culturally-competent affirming services that respond to urgent community needs. This funding is administered by the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene in partnership with the NYC Unity Project and the Citizens Committee for New city. The Empowerment Fund addresses persistent barriers that transgender and gender non-conforming and non-binary New Yorkers face when accessing healthcare, legal protections, and community-based support. Through this investment, the city is strengthening a network

of community-based providers that many gender non-conforming New Yorkers rely on for care, safety, and stability. This year, we are proud to share that New York City Men Teach, a program of the Young Men's Initiatives, also celebrated its 10th year anniversary. NYC Men Teach is a partnership between YMI, the public schools, and the City University for New York, which aims to improve the diversity of the teaching workforce. Mens Teach is open to all academically qualified students interested in teaching within the New York City public school system, but through recruitment efforts specifically targeted– we specifically target Black, Latino, and Asian men. The program focuses on recruiting students into teacher education programs and assisting them through graduation, certification, and the hiring process. Supports include intensive advisement, certification exam support, academic support, and financial assistance. Uh, Men's Teach is truly, uh, changing the landscape of education in the city. Through this program the public schools have successfully recruited over 5,000 educators who identify as men of color since 2016, strengthening classrooms while reinforcing public schools as a

destination for purpose-driven educators committed to our students and communities. Just last month, the YMI, in partnership with public schools and CUNY, hosted the 10-year anniversary event in Brooklyn at BRIC, and recognized and celebrated the accomplishments of this amazing program, as well as looked to the future of diverse recruitment. In regard to our training, we have spent, as I previously mentioned, time working to implement Local Law 13 of 2024, requiring the creation and administration of anti-racism training for all human services contractors in New York City who provide direct services to the public. In this fiscal year, we have worked in partnership with the CUNY School of Professional Students Office of Innovative Learning Solutions on course design, development, infrastructure, and hosting, uh, and more in preparation for its launch. We aim to finalize and launch this training by the end of this fiscal year. As of today, MOERJ Central has a current headcount of 38 with 26 active staff. Our office is small but mighty and committed to racial and gender equity and to continuing to tackle disparities in our communities. Many of us come from, live in, and have

experiences within the communities we are focused on serving through our work and come from areas as diverse as nonprofit, government, academia, and the private sector. As was mentioned by Chair Nurse, fiscal year '25, the budget provided was $8 million– a little over $8 million. In fiscal year '26, the preliminary budget currently provides $5,627,000. As discussions continue with OMB ahead of the executive budget, we aim to secure program funds included in our own pre— included in our previous fiscal year budget. As we look forward and I continue to settle into my role, as the Commissioner for MOERJ, I recognize the unique nature of this position in office, and more specifically, the opportunity to build on this strong foundation to ensure equity reaches every corner of government and informs discussions about how city prior— about city priorities and how they are implemented. I'm excited to continue advancing equity in government. We look forward to releasing this preliminary citywide racial equity plan, implementing its work, and measuring as well as reporting on our progress, releasing our first-ever New York City-specific true cost of living measure, and equally important, activating it as a

tool to inform policy and deliver services and influence budget decisions, beginning our anti-racism training to support thousands of human service provider employees who serve and interact with residents every day, and continuing to invest in young people, particularly young people of color and LGBT+ communities to tackle disparities experienced by their communities and ensure that all New Yorkers have the conditions of thriving. In closing, I thank you all for the opportunity to speak with you about the work of the Office of Equity and Racial Justice. We look forward to working every day as part of this administration to ensure that New Yorkers can continue to live, work, play, and thrive. Appreciate the support of this committee and many council members in ensuring that the issues of equity continue to remain on the forefront of the mind of many New Yorkers, and I thank you and welcome your questions.

Thank you so much, Commissioner. I'm going to jump right into it. We're going to start with looking at just overall budget. We'll go into headcount. We'll touch a little bit on the equity plan and true cost of living, and then

we'll talk a little bit about programming. So, um, as you mentioned in your testimony, we have seen reductions in your budget, and a lot of this is labeled as program funding adjustments where according to OMB, is a transfer of funds to other city agencies that are partnering with you all for MOERJ programming. So related to that, what programs were targeted by these transfers? What is the total funding level, and what agencies are you all partnering with where this funding is being reallocated towards or allocated towards?

Chair Nurse, thank you so much for the question. And as you mentioned, I would just also add it's part and parcel of business. Oftentimes in partnership with other agencies, money is transferred and directly allocated to those programs. And I'll take you through a list of some. I'm happy to go through more, and there's some as an addendum to the testimony as well. Let me just— so in total it was $551,184 that was transferred. Some examples include— let's start with the true cost of living measure. I spoke to what that is, the Racial Justice Charter Mandate to develop the city's first actual cost for what it– measuring of

the cost to not only meet needs, but live with dignity in the city. This is a collaboration with New York City Opportunity, DSS, HRA, and the Urban Institute. The funding that was transferred to cover costs was $200,000. This funding went to support things like methodology development, data collection and analysis, calculating costs for various groups, et cetera. Another example of that transfer was from the NYC Unity Project. The transfer amount was $150,000, and this was money for a partnership with, MOCJ, the Office for— MOCJ, excuse me, Office for the Prevention of Hate Crimes, the– as part of the Unity Project launching these Unity Grants that invested in LGBTQ communities. If I may, two more examples, or is that— all right. From NYC Her Future, the Young Women's Empowerment Program, this program seeks to expand current services by launching a comprehensive mental health and wellness initiative designed to support girls in middle and high school. The expansion of this program creates self-safe and culturally responsive trauma-informed spaces where students can build resilience and strengthen emotional well-being. This programming also includes a workshop and a culminating event. The program

expansion is projected to serve 300 students, and $40,000 of funding was transferred to help that expansion. The expand— this– and this is a partnership through DOE. So the expanded scope of programming since the allocation was established, um, has ex— was— is due to– excuse me– an increased demand of cross-agency engagement with DOE partners. So the additional funding will further support partnership with both Public Schools Office of Safety and Youth Development and continue to adequately support the scale, reach, and operational requirements of activities aligned with NYC HERS core priorities.

And then for— did you mention, sorry if you— if I missed it, the young men— young men's initiative transfer to the admin? I think it says the funds went to DSS. Did you mention that in that list just now?
Oh, I'm coming to it, but I can hop to it right now.
Okay.
Just so I'm clear, Chair, which allocation– is this the $325,000?

Okay. Perfect. I'm going to start, and then I have here with me, as I said, the Executive Director of NYC Her Future. So this transfer represented, in fact, was a transfer to NYC Her Future for programming. And after— excuse me— after conversation, it was determined that NYC Her Future did not require that full use of funding, and so some of those funds were transferred back. Young Men's Initiative plans to use that funding for, uh, men's health— sorry, there's a lot of pages here— and that is a program that is geared towards supporting a pipeline of mental health providers amongst men of color.

Okay, great. And then for the, the four offices, the NYC Her Future, Commission of Gender Equity, New York City Unity Project, and Young Men's Initiative, what's the headcount on, on these four offices?

Okay, thank you for the question. I stated that MOERJ has a budgeted head— sorry, Near NYC Her Future has six with, uh, one current vacancy. Unity Project currently has two, two lines, both of which are full. And then, Chair,

please excuse me, there's a few different papers here–
[interposing] Take your time.

And I want to— I would want to make sure that I'm accurate to the– before the council. Let me start again. Young Men's Initiative has 17 lines that spans across several different agencies, right, with four current vacancies. The Commission on Gender Equity has 13 for a total headcount, with two current— with two of them currently being vacant. NYC Her Future, as I said before, has six of a budgeted headcount, with one vacant. And I was correct in my previous assertion of the Unity Project having two.
And those are full?
And those are full. Thank you.
Understood. And so my understanding is as of January 2026, your vacancy rate went up to 31 percent. You have a budgeted headcount of 38 with a little more than 11 vacancies if my math is right.
12 vacancies.
12 vacancies, thank you. Are there any roles that are more difficult to hire than others?

I— thank you for the question, Councilmember. I haven't thought of that in that framing, so that's why I'm taking a moment to pause. I will say this, currently we have four posted, right? We are hiring for a policy director of program and two other are in media. You know, we are lucky that people are excited about working with and for this administration and this agency specifically. We have these positions posted on our website online and have received a lot of interest. So, and we're going to go through that process of the engagement and interviewing process. So currently we have not had, during my tenure, a hard time hiring for them. It's just the time of what it takes to engage folks and bring them on board.
And then, you were— were you all subject to the two-for-one hiring freeze in the former admin?
I can't speak to the— I'm sorry.
Were you subject to the hiring– the two-for-one hiring freeze under the former administration?
We were not.

You were not. Okay, so for the— you have four posted, but you have 12 vacancies. How do you see, since you weren't subject to the hiring freeze, how are you seeing your ability to fill these vacancies here?
Yeah, I– Commissioner go ahead.
So I'll start with we're moving forward with these forward and ongoing conversations with
Okay, right. And so have you all been instructed to find a 50 percent reduction in your vacancies?
So I would say that we have the Chief Savings Officer as we're mandated, which is Delilah here. We are still in conversation with OMB, and to my understanding— feel free.

Yeah, I'm more than happy to chime in. So we are mandated– we

are required, right, to go through the process, but we are in discussion with OMB. I would just add, you know, we're a new agency, so we're trying to work with our partners at the Office of Management and Budget to just get creative and really ensure we can, you know– as we are continuing to build, we don't run into major issues in just delivering on our mandates and doing the work that we need to do. So there's still ongoing discussion on what that, you know, may or may not look like.
Okay. Understand every— we know that everyone's in ongoing– oh sorry, we need to swear you in. I apologize.
Hello. Thank you. Would you mind raising your right hand, please? And do you swear to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, and that also what you said was that?
I, I do, and yes, it was.
Thank you so much. Apologize.

Thank you. Okay, so you've been asked to go through this exercise. Should

you need to complete the exercise and be subject to it, where do you see the overall impact being, both in terms of program or specific functions or job titles?

Sure. Thank you for the question. Just to help frame that, I think it's helpful to step back to something I said earlier in my testimony of how we go about the work, right? There is the structural shifts that we see through the implement— execution and implementation of things like the true cost of living and the preliminary racial equity plan. There's our programs, which I was able to highlight a bit of, and then also our culture shifts that we see through training. So thus far, with the staff that we have, we've been able to move forward and don't foresee any hurdles to ensuring that we move forward with our charter mandates. Similarly, each of our units, as well as MOERJ Central, has been able to move forward in partnerships and collaboration with other city agencies to ensure that the important programs go forward. And we are on the cusp of finishing the trainings that will go for each of the human services— the, excuse me, the agencies that engage

with externally. So we're confident that we can make this happen under the framing that we have, and that will hit— make sure that we meet all of our obligations under charter mandates.

Yeah, no, we know, you know, all agencies are doing the best they can with the little that they got. They could always have more, right? And always do more work. And so if there are particular areas that would be vulnerable, given all of the, the programmatic work you all have and charter-mandated requirements, it would be helpful for the council to know, because we want to advocate for you. We're not trying to get you. We're trying to support you, because this is work that New Yorkers voted for and that we support. Okay, for racial— I'm just going to ask about racial equity programming and then I'll open it up. So if members have questions, let me know. We did talk about racial equity. We're not going to drill down into it. We know you are saying that you're planning to publish those within the first 100 days. Are we still on track for that first 100 days?
Thank you for the question, Chair. We are still on track for the first 100 days.
And how many staff currently in MOERJ are explicitly assigned to work on the REPs?

At this current time— so I, I'm going to fully answer your question, but I think it's helpful to provide context. This is a priority for this office. So we have nine, um, Equity Planning Managers. You've heard me use the abbreviation EPMs, who the vast majority, if not all of their time, is focused on this plan. And because, again, this plan is a priority for the office, it is some of the Deputy Commissioner's time. It is some of my time. It is some of other senior advisors' time as well. So I want to add that to give further shape and frame to the amount of folks who are also working on this.
That is helpful to know. And do you have any vacancies? Are any of your vacancies related to the racial equity plan work?

Thank you for the question. So we started– I guess they started the

calendar year with 10 EPMs and then, prior to my coming on board, one– we are now at nine.
Okay, so we– so that one we shouldn't lose in the vacancy potential cut. Okay, and the– you said the true cost of living is in the coming weeks. We're on track for the March 31st deadline.
Thank you for the question. It is— so it's my understanding that it will be coming out by the end of this month.
Great. And how many people are assigned to this particular piece of work?

Similar to with the racial equity plan, there are several people tasked in the office specifically for this. We have about two people who specifically work on this as the majority of their work, and it is part and parcel of time of the Deputy Commissioner, part of my time, and we're part of this as a partnership through the Urban Institute, and other agencies in putting this together.

And I know for both the prelim— the draft racial equity plan and the true cost of living, I know that there's been so much

interest and wanting to get that over the finish line and disappointment with the last administration. So I imagine you want to kind of come out– come out the gate telling everyone what you got. What are some of the plans you have and do you have budget for kind of getting the word out about what you have published and getting feedback?

Yeah. Thank you for that. So I'd say we have a multifaceted approach to how we're going to do engagement. First and foremost, CORE, we will partner with CORE, but CORE will be taking the lead in community engagement in regards to the racial equity plan. Our plan and engagement also will be to directly speak to stakeholders to do presentations and engagements across city agencies, and of course, we will provide ongoing technical assistance. Similar with the true cost of living, the goal— this tool is only as good as its use. So our goal is to, one, first and foremost, ensure that there's full digestion across city agencies so they have an understanding of the possibilities with this tool. And as well to work with Urban Institute and other academic partners, as well as the Federation for Protestant Welfare

Agencies. FPWA has been a leader on this to ensure that across the city folks have an understanding of the possibilities for this tool.

I'm gonna open it up to some of my council colleagues, but I– and then I'll come back to talk about some program, but I do want to just appreciate and acknowledge the addendum you put in here, or the appendix, I don't know what it's called, for the— some of the investments. I know we had talked about– there was a lot of questions about the Bronx investments, so I really appreciate the detailed information. We really appreciate that. I have Council Member Stevens.

Hello, good afternoon. I guess the first question I have, I just wanted to start with, like, Men Teach, which is one of these programs that I really like, and want to just ask the question around, like, even in this time where we're having issues with– like, when we're talking about class size mandate, we're not talking about how this is like stretching the workforce really thin. And just specifically in the Bronx, we always have had issues with retaining teachers, and especially in the Bronx, I just always have felt like

we need more men teachers and men of color, obviously. And just thinking about how— and how this partnership is looking, and when you are recruiting these young men of color to be in this program, are we prioritizing boroughs like the Bronx to help with placements? And what does that partnership look like with DOE?

Good afternoon, Council Member Stevens. I don't know if you came in when I was initially speaking, but I'm joined here with the Director Natifa Forde for NYC Her Future. We previously served as the head of YLI. And so because we learned the lesson the first time, I wanted to make sure that we were able to speak with specificity. So I brought backup today.
